title: r/Baking
tagline: Home bakers and dessert lovers; local buyers ask for custom orders.
audience: Home bakers sharing wins, plus a sweet-toothed audience that upvotes anything glossy. For cottage bakers, the local angle is the play — commenters regularly ask if you sell nearby.
overview:
A big, appreciative community where beautiful bakes travel fast: laminated doughs, glossy ganache, first-attempt sourdoughs celebrated alongside showpiece cakes. The audience is part baker, part admirer — plenty of members are here purely for the pictures.

For a home bakery, the reach is portfolio rather than pipeline: cake doesn't ship. But presence compounds — a baker whose work keeps appearing, who mentions their city naturally, becomes findable to the local lurkers who will eventually need a birthday cake.
discussions:
Showpiece posts: decorated cakes, laminated pastries, glossy tarts
Technique troubleshooting: dense crumb, split buttercream, sunken middles
Recipe requests and "what did I do wrong" threads
Cottage-baking business questions: pricing, licensing, first market stalls
Holiday bake threads — seasonal spikes of ambition and disaster
loves:
Clean process shots and honest crumb photos
Technique answers from bakers who clearly do this daily
Before-and-after journeys: the first sourdough vs the fiftieth
dislikes:
Obvious ads for bakeries with no participation
Recipe-hoarding — refusing to share when asked reads as pure promotion
Stock-photo-perfect posts that feel commercial rather than personal
rules:
Self-promotion is limited; business posts belong in designated spaces
Cottage food laws vary by region — legal advice threads are informational, not authoritative
Recipe-sharing culture is expected; posts that gate everything behind a link get removed
approach: Use it as your public portfolio and technique reputation, mention your city naturally in comments, and crosspost your best work to your city's subreddit — that's where the actual customers live. Know your cottage food laws and state plainly what you offer.
tags: baking, cake, cookies, dessert, bakery, food

title: #customcakes
tagline: People planning events search this tag to find bakers near them.
audience: Event planners in the most literal sense: people with a birthday, wedding, or shower on the calendar and a cake-shaped hole in the plan. They search with a date and a budget already in mind.
overview:
Cake buying is local, occasion-driven, and visual — three things that make Instagram its natural marketplace. The #customcakes tag and its local variants are where people with an event on the calendar go to find a baker whose style matches the party in their head.

Buyers arrive with specifics: a date, a headcount, a theme, sometimes a screenshot of someone else's cake. The bakers who win treat their grid as a menu organized by occasion, and their DMs as a booking desk.
discussions:
Finished-cake reveals tagged by occasion: birthdays, weddings, showers
Theme and trend content: vintage piping, minimalist designs, character cakes
Flavor menus and filling combinations in captions and comments
Behind-the-scenes: stacking, transport nerves, delivery-day videos
Booking logistics: lead times, deposits, service areas
loves:
Grids organized like menus — they're shopping by style and occasion
City and service area stated visibly; local is everything
Price anchors ("cakes from $X") that let them self-qualify before DMing
dislikes:
No location anywhere — a perfect cake three states away is just a picture
Total price mystery, which fills DMs with dead-end inquiries
Grids mixing personal life with product until neither reads clearly
rules:
Local discoverability depends on city tags and location tagging — the generic tag alone won't be found
Food business regulations (licensing, labeling) vary by region and apply to what you claim
DM-based ordering means response time is part of the product
approach: Always tag your city and use local tag variants — an out-of-town like is worthless, a local follow is a future order. Organize story highlights by occasion, anchor your pricing publicly, and treat DM response speed as part of your reputation.

title: r/CottageFood
tagline: The legal and practical side of selling food from a home kitchen.
audience: Home food sellers navigating cottage food laws, licensing, labelling and insurance. Small but exceptionally useful — this is the room that keeps you legal.
overview:
Where the unglamorous but essential part of food selling gets discussed: what your state or country allows, what labelling is required, whether you need a commercial kitchen, how insurance works.

For anyone selling food, getting this wrong is the fastest way to lose a business, which makes this community disproportionately valuable relative to its size.
discussions:
Cottage food law by region and what it permits
Labelling requirements and allergen declarations
When a commercial kitchen becomes necessary
Insurance and liability
Pricing that accounts for compliance costs
loves:
Region-specific, accurate legal information
Honest accounts of inspections and what was asked
Practical labelling examples
dislikes:
Advice to ignore regulations
Confidently wrong legal claims
Self-promotion
rules:
Legal information is shared as experience, not professional advice
Self-promotion restricted
Encouraging non-compliance is moderated
approach: Read this before you sell a single item. Knowing your local cottage food rules — and saying so on your listings — is both protection and a selling point to cautious buyers.
tags: food, baking, cottage food, legal, licensing, home kitchen, jam, sauce

title: #BakeTok
tagline: Decorating videos are among the most-watched content anywhere on the app.
audience: An enormous audience watching things get iced, piped and assembled. Local buyers find home bakeries through this feed constantly.
overview:
Baking content is a cornerstone category, and decorating in particular — piping, glazing, the moment a plain cake becomes finished — holds attention like almost nothing else.

For a home baker the local angle is what converts: viewers who discover you and happen to be nearby become customers, so making your city obvious matters more than raw views.
discussions:
Cake and cookie decorating in close-up
Recipe walkthroughs
Order-prep and bake-day marathons
Disaster and rescue videos
Business-side content about running a home bakery
loves:
Satisfying decorating moments filmed close
Realistic kitchens rather than studio sets
Honest fails, which perform extremely well
dislikes:
Recipes that clearly don't work
Overproduced content that feels commercial
Ignoring the comments asking about ordering
rules:
Commercial music licensing applies
Food safety claims and cottage-law compliance still apply offline
Commerce features require eligibility
approach: Put your city in your bio and mention it in videos. Views from across the country are worthless to a baker — one local viewer who orders a birthday cake is worth ten thousand distant ones.
tags: baking, cake, cookies, dessert, decorating, bakery

title: r/hotsauce
tagline: Collectors who own thirty bottles and are hunting the next one.
audience: Hot sauce enthusiasts who collect, trade and review obsessively. Small-batch and craft producers are actively sought out here.
overview:
A collector community in the truest sense — members photograph their shelves, trade bottles by post, and review new releases in detail. Craft producers are welcomed rather than resented.

The defining trait is a preference for interesting over merely hot, which favours small makers doing something distinctive with fermentation or unusual peppers.
discussions:
Collection and shelf photos
New release reviews and first impressions
Fermentation technique and recipes
Pepper varieties and sourcing
Bottle trades and swaps
loves:
Genuinely distinctive flavour rather than heat for its own sake
Fermentation detail and process transparency
Small makers who engage as enthusiasts
dislikes:
Heat-only marketing with no flavour behind it
Undisclosed producer accounts
Extract-based sauces marketed as craft
rules:
Producer participation usually requires disclosure
Self-promotion restricted to designated threads
Reviews should disclose free or gifted bottles
approach: Disclose that you make sauce, then talk fermentation like the enthusiast you are. This community rewards process transparency, and a bottle trade with a few regulars generates more honest reviews than any advertising.
tags: hot sauce, fermented, chilli, condiment, spicy, craft food

title: r/coffee
tagline: Serious coffee people who spend heavily and taste critically.
audience: Coffee enthusiasts from pour-over hobbyists to home baristas with expensive setups. They buy beans constantly and judge roasters on real criteria.
overview:
A large, technically-minded community focused on brewing and beans. Members discuss origin, processing, roast date and extraction with real precision, and they buy from small roasters routinely.

Roast date matters enormously here — freshness is the single most scrutinised claim, and getting it right is table stakes.
discussions:
Bean recommendations by origin and process
Brewing method and extraction troubleshooting
Grinder and machine advice
Roaster recommendations and reviews
Subscription comparisons
loves:
Roast dates printed clearly, not best-before dates
Origin and processing transparency
Roasters who talk honestly about what a coffee tastes like
dislikes:
Vague blend descriptions with no origin information
Stale beans sold as fresh
Marketing language over tasting notes
rules:
Self-promotion restricted; roaster participation typically requires disclosure
Affiliate links are not permitted
Reviews should disclose gifted product
approach: If you're selling coffee, print the roast date and state the origin — this audience checks both first. Participate on brewing questions rather than promoting, and let the specificity of your product pages do the work.
tags: coffee, beans, roast, brewing, espresso, subscription
